problem: LLM-based task planners mostly do not close the loop, so the policy does not improve across episodes. Reflection-based methods such as Reflexion reflect on the whole long trajectory, which makes it hard to locate the error.
motivation: LLM policies for robotics need to improve from environmental feedback without gradient training. Long trajectories dilute the reflection signal, while hierarchical decomposition offers shorter, more focused units to reflect on.
key_idea: Use an LLM as a goal-conditioned hierarchical policy (a high-level policy proposes sub-goals online, a low-level policy executes them). Reflect separately on the goal sequence and on each sub-trajectory (Hindsight Modular Reflection), and retrieve the reflections from memory as context.
insight: Shorter, modular reflection inputs help the LLM find its mistakes. In the ablation, RAHL-HMR beats RAHL-Reflexion (full-trajectory reflection), especially on long, text-heavy ALFWorld and HotpotQA. Tag guidance ([Goal]/[Think]/[Action]/[Finish]) matters: RAHL w/o Tag is clearly worse. Verbal reflections beat simply retrying with raw failed trajectories. GPT-3.5 acting with GPT-4 doing the HMR outperforms plain GPT-3.5, and even GPT-4 on HotpotQA (reported in a figure only).
method: Hierarchical in-context policy: a high-level LLM policy generates one goal at a time from the task and the episode history, and a low-level LLM policy generates actions to reach that goal. Goals are regenerated online only when the finisher returns yes.
Tag-guided prompting: the prompt uses [Goal], [Think], [Action] and [Finish] tags to inject a human-like reasoning flow. Few-shot examples are full successful trajectories.

Finisher: an LLM check on the sub-trajectory since the last completed goal that decides whether the current goal is achieved. If so, the high-level policy is queried; otherwise the low-level policy acts again.

Hindsight Modular Reflection: the low-level policy must complete the proposed goals even if they are wrong. After a failed episode, the low-level policy reflects on each sub-trajectory and the high-level policy reflects on the goal sequence, each producing 1-2 sentence reflections.

Memory and retrieval: short-term memory holds the current trajectory. Long-term memory has separate high- and low-level stores of (task/sub-task description → reflection) pairs. Retrieval embeds the query and takes the top-2 nearest keys, whose reflections are added to the prompt.

setting.backbone: GPT-3.5-turbo (frozen, default); GPT-4 variants in ablation; GPT-4-turbo (image analyst) and GPT-4o (decision-maker) on the SPOT robot
setting.training_data: none (training-free, in-context; 2 few-shot full trajectories per task, plus reflection examples)
setting.observation: text observations (ALFWorld, Webshop, HotpotQA); on the real robot, two head-mounted cameras analysed by GPT-4-turbo
setting.action_space: text-level plans/commands (environment text actions); on SPOT, LLM-chosen high-level navigation commands
setting.simulator: ALFWorld (text), Webshop, HotpotQA; real Boston Dynamics SPOT for the hardware demo
setting.privileged: none (the reward or success signal is used across episodes for reflection)

numbers_note: The ablations (RAHL-Retry/Reflexion/w/o Tag, GPT-4 variants) are reported only in figures, so no numbers are extracted. The SPOT experiment is qualitative. The split label 'val' is a guess because the paper does not name splits.
results: With GPT-3.5-turbo, RAHL reaches 67/69/37% Pass@1 and 87/83/57% at 5 episodes on ALFWorld/Webshop/HotpotQA. It beats Reflexion in all cases (78/28/47% at 5 episodes) and beats ExpeL on all three at 5 episodes. Retroformer is better on ALFWorld at 5 episodes (100%), and ADaPT is better at Pass@1 on ALFWorld (71%). The largest gain is on Webshop (83% vs 41% for ExpeL at episode 5).
limitations: Still underperforms trained large models and hits bottlenecks on complex tasks such as HotpotQA, because LLM prior knowledge can be biased and stubborn.
